docs.title: COHO Ontology Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome to the COHO documentation!

You can find descriptions of the standard ontology engineering workflows here.

docs.title: COHO Workflows
docs.text:
COHO is built with owlmake: a single program, om, with no Docker, Java or Python to set up. The whole build is described by owlmake.yaml at the top of the repository.

  • Installing owlmake
  • Daily Editors Workflow
  • Release Workflow
  • Build configuration
  • Imports management
  • Components management
  • Quality control and Continuous Integration
  • Managing the documentation
  • Repository overview

docs.title: Build configuration
docs.text: COHO is built with owlmake. The repository was created with the Ontology Development Kit (ODK) and owlmake builds it the way ODK 1.6.1 did, producing the same files, but from one configuration file and one program.

docs.title: Installing owlmake
docs.text:
1. Download the om binary for your machine from the owlmake releases page (for example om-macos-arm64 or om-linux-amd64).
  2. Rename it to om, make it executable, and put it on your PATH:
chmod +x om-macos-arm64
mv om-macos-arm64 ~/.local/bin/om

om --version should now print a version of at least the min_owlmake_version stated in owlmake.yaml. Nothing else needs installing: no Docker, Java or ROBOT.

docs.title: owlmake.yaml
docs.text:
owlmake.yaml, at the top of the repository, holds what this repository decided and nothing else:

  • emulate_odk_version — the standard build the file is written against. Everything the options below imply (release pipelines, import extraction, reports, QC checks) is that standard build, which is built into owlmake.
  • id, title, uribase, github_org, repo — the ontology's identity.
  • namespaces — the IRI prefixes of COHO's own terms (http://www.ebi.ac.uk/coho/ and http://www.ebi.ac.uk/coho#). The base release keeps only axioms about these, and the QC report checks only these. Without it the standard build assumes <uribase>/COHO, which matches nothing here: the base release was empty until 2026-09-22.
  • release_artefacts, primary_release, export_formats — which release files are made, and in which formats.
  • import_group — the ontologies COHO imports terms from (see Imports management).
  • components — the parts of COHO generated from ROBOT templates (see Components management).
  • robot_report — the quality control checks (see Quality control).

The options have the names and meanings they have in an ODK configuration, so the ODK configuration reference applies to them.

A change to owlmake.yaml takes effect the next time om runs. After adding or removing an import or a component, run om update-repo as well: it updates the edit file's imports and the XML catalog to match, and creates the placeholder files the first build reads. om make --plan-only prints the whole build the file amounts to, and om make --list-targets every target that can be built.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Run these from anywhere in the repository:

Command What it does om make test IMP=false Run the quality control checks om make prepare_release -B IMP=false Build every release file and copy them to the top of the repository om refresh-imports Download the imported ontologies again and rebuild the import modules om make recreate-components Rebuild the components from their templates om update-repo Bring the edit file's imports, the XML catalog and placeholder files into step with owlmake.yaml om make coho.obo Build one file

IMP=false reuses the import modules committed in src/ontology/imports instead of rebuilding them, and MIR=false reuses ontologies already downloaded. -B rebuilds everything, whether or not it looks up to date.

docs.title: Building something in a way of your own
docs.text: A file that the standard build does not make, or makes differently from how COHO needs it, is described under a targets key in owlmake.yaml, as the file it makes, what it needs, and the steps that make it. See the owlmake documentation.

docs.title: Editors Workflow
docs.text:
The editors workflow is one of the formal workflows to ensure that the ontology is developed correctly according to ontology engineering principles. There are a few different editors workflows:

  1. Local editing workflow: Editing the ontology in your local environment by hand, using tools such as Protégé, ROBOT templates or DOSDP patterns.
  2. Completely automated data pipeline (GitHub Actions)
  3. DROID workflow

This document only covers the first editing workflow, but more will be added in the future

docs.title: Local editing workflow
docs.text:
Workflow requirements:

  • git
  • github
  • owlmake
  • editing tool of choice, e.g. Protégé, your favourite text editor, etc

docs.title: 1. Create issue
docs.text: Ensure that there is a ticket on your issue tracker that describes the change you are about to make. While this seems optional, this is a very important part of the social contract of building an ontology - no change to the ontology should be performed without a good ticket, describing the motivation and nature of the intended change.

docs.title: 2. Update main branch
docs.text:
In your local environment (e.g. your laptop), make sure you are on the main (prev. master) branch and ensure that you have all the upstream changes, for example:

git checkout main
git pull

docs.title: 3. Create feature branch
docs.text:
Create a new branch. Per convention, we try to use meaningful branch names such as: - issue23removeprocess (where issue 23 is the related issue on GitHub) - issue26addcontributor - release20210101 (for releases)

On your command line, this looks like this:

git checkout -b issue23removeprocess

docs.title: 4. Perform edit
docs.text:
Using your editor of choice, perform the intended edit. For example:

Protégé

  1. Open src/ontology/coho-edit.owl in Protégé
  2. Make the change
  3. Save the file

TextEdit

  1. Open src/ontology/coho-edit.owl in TextEdit (or Sublime, Atom, Vim, Nano)
  2. Make the change
  3. Save the file

Consider the following when making the edit.

  1. According to our development philosophy, the only places that should be manually edited are:
    • src/ontology/coho-edit.owl
    • Any ROBOT templates you chose to use (the TSV files only)
    • Any DOSDP data tables you chose to use (the TSV files, and potentially the associated patterns)
    • components (anything in src/ontology/components), see here.
  2. Imports should not be edited (any edits will be flushed out with the next update). However, refreshing imports is a potentially breaking change - and is discussed elsewhere.
  3. Changes should usually be small. Adding or changing 1 term is great. Adding or changing 10 related terms is ok. Adding or changing 100 or more terms at once should be considered very carefully.

docs.title: 4. Check the Git diff
docs.text:
This step is very important. Rather than simply trusting your change had the intended effect, we should always use a git diff as a first pass for sanity checking.

In our experience, having a visual git client like GitHub Desktop or sourcetree is really helpful for this part. In case you prefer the command line:

git status
git diff

docs.title: 5. Quality control
docs.text: Now it's time to run your quality control checks. This can either happen locally (5a) or through your continuous integration system (7/5b).

docs.title: 5a. Local testing
docs.text:
If you chose to run your test locally:

om make test IMP=false
This will run the whole set of configured quality control checks including your change. IMP=false reuses the committed import modules rather than rebuilding them.

docs.title: 6. Pull request
docs.text:
When you are happy with the changes, you commit your changes to your feature branch, push them upstream (to GitHub) and create a pull request. For example:

git add NAMEOFCHANGEDFILES
git commit -m "Added biological process term #12"
git push -u origin issue23removeprocess

Then you go to your project on GitHub, and create a new pull request from the branch, for example: https://github.com/EBISPOT/cohort-ontology/pulls

There is a lot of great advise on how to write pull requests, but at the very least you should: - mention the tickets affected: see #23 to link to a related ticket, or fixes #23 if, by merging this pull request, the ticket is fixed. Tickets in the latter case will be closed automatically by GitHub when the pull request is merged. - summarise the changes in a few sentences. Consider the reviewer: what would they want to know right away. - If the diff is large, provide instructions on how to review the pull request best (sometimes, there are many changed files, but only one important change).

docs.title: 7/5b. Continuous Integration Testing
docs.text: If you didn't run and local quality control checks (see 5a), the Continuous Integration (CI) on GitHub Actions runs them for you, see here. Once the pull request is created, the CI will automatically trigger. If all is fine, it will show up green, otherwise red.

docs.title: 8. Community review
docs.text:
Once all the automatic tests have passed, it is important to put a second set of eyes on the pull request. Ontologies are inherently social - as in that they represent some kind of community consensus on how a domain is organised conceptually. This seems high brow talk, but it is very important that as an ontology editor, you have your work validated by the community you are trying to serve (e.g. your colleagues, other contributors etc.). In our experience, it is hard to get more than one review on a pull request - two is great. You can set up GitHub branch protection to actually require a review before a pull request can be merged! We recommend this.

This step seems daunting to some hopefully under-resourced ontologies, but we recommend to put this high up on your list of priorities - train a colleague, reach out!

docs.title: 9. Merge and cleanup
docs.text: When the QC is green and the reviews are in (approvals), it is time to merge the pull request. After the pull request is merged, remember to delete the branch as well (this option will show up as a big button right after you have merged the pull request). If you have not done so, close all the associated tickets fixed by the pull request.

docs.title: 10. Changelog (Optional)
docs.text: It is sometimes difficult to keep track of changes made to an ontology. Some ontology teams opt to document changes in a changelog (simply a text file in your repository) so that when release day comes, you know everything you have changed. This is advisable at least for major changes (such as a new release system, a new pattern or template etc.).

docs.title: Updating the Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation for COHO is managed in two places (relative to the repository root):

  1. The docs directory contains all the files that pertain to the content of the documentation (more below)
  2. the mkdocs.yaml file contains the documentation config, in particular its navigation bar and theme.

The documentation is hosted using GitHub pages, on a special branch of the repository (called gh-pages). It is important that this branch is never deleted - it contains all the files GitHub pages needs to render and deploy the site. It is also important to note that the gh-pages branch should never be edited manually. All changes to the docs happen inside the docs directory on the main branch.

docs.title: Changing content
docs.text:
All the documentation is contained in the docs directory, and is managed in Markdown. Markdown is a very simple and convenient way to produce text documents with formatting instructions, and is very easy to learn - it is also used, for example, in GitHub issues. This is a normal editing workflow:

  1. Open the .md file you want to change in an editor of choice (a simple text editor is often best).
  2. Perform the edit and save the file
  3. Commit the file to a branch, and create a pull request as usual.
  4. If your development team likes your changes, merge the docs into main branch.
  5. The documentation is deployed (see below)

docs.title: Deploy the documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is deployed by GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/docs.yml) whenever a change reaches the main branch; the workflow can also be started by hand from the repository's Actions tab. Give GitHub a few minutes, and the change is visible at https://EBISPOT.github.io/cohort-ontology/.

To look at the site before merging, install mkdocs with the mkdocs-material theme and run mkdocs serve --config-file mkdocs.yaml from the top of the repository.

docs.title: Running the checks
docs.text:
om make test IMP=false

This runs, over the edit file with its imports and components:

  • a reasoner check: the ontology must be consistent, with no unsatisfiable classes;
  • the ROBOT report, failing on anything it grades ERROR. The report is written to src/ontology/reports/coho-edit.owl-obo-report.tsv;
  • the constraint violation checks described below, over both the edit file and coho-full.owl;
  • a check that the released ontology is within the OWL 2 DL profile;
  • a check of the ID ranges in src/ontology/coho-idranges.owl.

IMP=false reuses the committed import modules rather than rebuilding them.

docs.title: Continuous Integration
docs.text: The same checks run on GitHub Actions for every pull request and every push to main. The workflow is .github/workflows/qc.yml: it installs the owlmake version named by OWLMAKE_VERSION and runs om make test. To build with a newer owlmake, change that version there.

docs.title: Constraint violation checks
docs.text: We can define custom checks using SPARQL. SPARQL queries define bad modelling patterns (missing labels, misspelt URIs, and many more) in the ontology. If these queries return any results, then the build will fail.

docs.title: Steps to add a constraint violation check:
docs.text:
1. Add the SPARQL query in src/sparql. The name of the file should end with -violation.sparql. Please give a name that helps to understand which violation the query wants to check.

  2. Add the name of the new file (without the -violation.sparql part) to the custom_sparql_checks list under report in owlmake.yaml:

    report:
  custom_sparql_checks:
  - name-of-the-file-check

The check is part of om make test from then on.

COHO's own checks include subset-example: a cohort in the EGA, GWAS, MetaboLights, PRIDE or PGS subset must have an example study (IAO:0000112) from that resource, an EGAS, GCST, MTBLS, PXD or PGS accession respectively; placeholder terms, whose curation status is uncurated, are exempt. catalogue-subset does the same for the catalogue subsets: a term in the GEC subset must carry a cross-reference to its entry in the Global Exposome Cohort Catalogue (and a term with such a cross-reference must be in the subset), and a term in the IHCC subset must be a member of the International Health Cohorts Consortium (COHO:0002701), whose atlas the listing is. participants-evidence holds the numbers of participants to their evidence: every numberOfParticipants, numberOfCases or numberOfControls assertion must be a non-negative integer that carries the source stating it (oboInOwl:hasDbXref on the axiom), and a term has at most one number per property.

A check that should be reported but not fail the build goes instead into src/ontology/profile.txt, the QC report's rule set (custom_profile: true in owlmake.yaml): a line WARN file:../sparql/your-check-report.sparql, with the query returning ?entity ?property ?value. The aggregation-membership check runs this way.

docs.title: The release workflow
docs.text:
The release workflow is based on GitHub releases and works as follows:

  1. Run a release with owlmake
  2. Review the release
  3. Merge to main branch
  4. Create a GitHub release

These steps are outlined in detail in the following.

docs.title: Run a release with owlmake
docs.text:
Preparation:

  1. Ensure that all your pull requests are merged into your main branch
  2. Make sure that all changes to main are committed to GitHub (git status should say that there are no modified files)
  3. Locally make sure you have the latest changes from main (git pull)
  4. Checkout a new branch (e.g. git checkout -b release-2021-01-01)
  5. You may or may not want to refresh your imports as part of your release strategy (see here)
  6. Make sure you have owlmake installed, at the version owlmake.yaml asks for or newer (om --version)

To actually run the release, you:

  1. Open a command line terminal window and navigate to the repository
  2. Run the release pipeline: om make prepare_release -B IMP=false. (Leave out IMP=false to rebuild the import modules from the imported ontologies as part of the release.)
  3. If everything went well, the output ends with published 12 release file(s) and done.

This will create all the specified release targets (OBO, OWL, JSON, and the variants, coho-full and coho-base) and copy them into your release directory (the top level of your repo). It also redraws the map in the README of where the cohorts recruited, docs/images/cohort-map.svg, from the release's data collection locations (src/scripts/cohort_map.py), and rewrites coho-cohorts.csv, the table of the cohorts and their metadata, from the edit file and its components (src/scripts/cohort_table.py). Commit both with the release files.

docs.title: Review the release
docs.text:
1. (Optional) Rough check. This step is frequently skipped, but for the more paranoid among us, this is a 3 minute additional effort for some peace of mind. Open the main release (coho.owl) in you favourite development environment (i.e. Protégé) and eyeball the hierarchy. We recommend two simple checks:
    1. Does the very top level of the hierarchy look ok? This means that all new terms have been imported/updated correctly.
    2. Does at least one change that you know should be in this release appear? For example, a new class. This means that the release was actually based on the recent edit file.
  2. Commit your changes to the branch and make a pull request
  3. In your GitHub pull request, review the following three files in detail (based on our experience):
    1. coho.obo - this reflects a useful subset of the whole ontology (everything that can be covered by OBO format). OBO format has that speaking for it: it is very easy to review!
    2. coho-base.owl - this reflects the asserted axioms in your ontology that you have actually edited.
    3. Ideally also take a look at coho-full.owl, which may reveal interesting new inferences you did not know about. Note that the diff of this file is sometimes quite large.
  4. Like with every pull request, we recommend to always employ a second set of eyes when reviewing a PR!

docs.title: Merge the main branch
docs.text: Once your CI checks have passed, and your reviews are completed, you can now merge the branch into your main branch (don't forget to delete the branch afterwards - a big button will appear after the merge is finished).

docs.title: Create a GitHub release
docs.text:
1. Go to your releases page on GitHub by navigating to your repository, and then clicking on releases (usually on the right, for example: https://github.com/EBISPOT/cohort-ontology/releases). Then click "Draft new release"
  2. As the tag version you need to choose the date on which your ontologies were build. You can find this, for example, by looking at the coho.obo file and check the data-version: property. The date needs to be prefixed with a v, so, for example v2020-02-06.
  3. You can write whatever you want in the release title, but we typically write the date again. The description underneath should contain a concise list of changes or term additions.
  4. Attach the release files, coho-cohorts.csv among them.
  5. Click "Publish release". Done.

docs.title: A check fails
docs.text: The release runs the same quality control checks as the test target. When one fails, the output names the check and what it found. Fix the edit file or the template the message points at, and run the release again.

docs.title: The map leaves a large country unshaded
docs.text: The map step prints the located countries it has no outline for. Only very small countries, such as Singapore, should be among them. A larger one means its name in the outlines (src/map/countries-110m.json) differs from its label in src/templates/gaz_xrefs.tsv: add the pair to OUTLINE_NAMES in src/scripts/cohort_map.py and run the release again.

docs.title: Repository structure
docs.text:
The main kinds of files in the repository:

  1. The build configuration, owlmake.yaml
  2. The edit file, src/ontology/coho-edit.owl: the only ontology file edited by hand
  3. Release files
  4. Imports
  5. Components

docs.title: Release files
docs.text: Release file are the file that are considered part of the official ontology release and to be used by the community. They are at the top of the repository: coho.owl and coho.obo (the primary release, the same as coho-full.owl), coho-full.owl (the ontology with its imports, classified) and coho-base.owl (only the axioms that belong to COHO itself). coho-cohorts.csv is the same cohorts as a table, one row per term (src/scripts/cohort_table.py).

docs.title: Imports
docs.text:
Imports are subsets of external ontologies that contain terms and axioms you would like to re-use in your ontology. These are considered "external", like dependencies in software development, and are not included in your "base" product, the release file which contains only those axioms that you personally maintain.

These are the current imports in COHO

Import URL Type ro http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/ro.owl slme omo http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/omo.owl mirror NCIT http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/NCIT.owl slme

See Imports management.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Components, in contrast to imports, are considered full members of the ontology. This means that any axiom in a component is also included in the ontology base - which means it is considered native to the ontology. While this sounds complicated, consider this: conceptually, no component should be part of more than one ontology. If that seems to be the case, we are most likely talking about an import. Components are often not needed for ontologies, but there are some use cases:

  1. There is an automated process that generates and re-generates a part of the ontology
  2. A part of the ontology is managed in ROBOT templates
  3. The expressivity of the component is higher than the format of the edit file. For example, people still choose to manage their ontology in OBO format (they should not) missing out on a lot of owl features. They may choose to manage logic that is beyond OBO in a specific OWL component.

These are the components in COHO

Filename Built from gaz_xrefs.owl src/templates/gaz_xrefs.tsv GWAS.owl src/templates/GWAS.csv MetaboLight.owl src/templates/MetaboLight.csv EGA.owl src/templates/EGA.csv PRIDE.owl src/templates/PRIDE.csv

See Components management.

docs.title: Update Imports Workflow
docs.text:
This page discusses how to update the contents of your imports, like adding or removing terms. To change which ontologies are imported, edit import_group in owlmake.yaml and run om update-repo, then refresh the imports; see Build configuration.

COHO imports terms from these ontologies, listed under import_group in owlmake.yaml:

Import URL Type ro http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/ro.owl slme omo http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/omo.owl mirror NCIT http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/NCIT.owl slme

Each has an import module, src/ontology/imports/<id>_import.owl, holding just the terms COHO uses and what the source ontology says about them. Import modules are never edited by hand: any edit is lost the next time the imports are refreshed.

docs.title: Importing a new term
docs.text:
Importing a new term is split into two sub-phases:

  1. Declaring the terms to be imported
  2. Refreshing imports dynamically

docs.title: Declaring terms to be imported
docs.text: There are two ways to declare terms that are to be imported from an external ontology. Both can be used in parallel.

docs.title: Protégé-based declaration
docs.text:
1. Open your ontology (edit file) in Protégé (5.5+).
  2. Select 'owl:Thing'
  3. Add a new class as usual.
  4. Paste the full iri in the 'Name:' field, for example, http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/NCIT_C61512.
  5. Click 'OK'

Now you can use this term for example to construct logical definitions. The next time the imports are refreshed (see how to refresh here), the metadata (labels, definitions, etc.) for this term are imported from the respective external source ontology and becomes visible in your ontology.

docs.title: Using term files
docs.text:
Every import has a term file associated with it, which can be found in the imports directory: for the NCIT import src/ontology/imports/NCIT_import.owl, it is src/ontology/imports/NCIT_terms.txt. You can add terms in there simply as a list:

NCIT:C61512
NCIT:C17005

Now you can run the refresh imports workflow and the two terms will be imported.

docs.title: Refresh imports
docs.text:
To rebuild the import modules so that they include any new terms you have added:

om refresh-imports

This downloads the imported ontologies again, so that the modules reflect their latest releases. NCIT is large, and this can take a while.

A single module is rebuilt by naming it:

om make imports/NCIT_import.owl -B IMP=true

If you wish to skip downloading the latest version of the source ontology and rebuild the module from the copy downloaded last time (kept in src/ontology/mirror, which is not committed), add MIR=false:

om make imports/NCIT_import.owl -B IMP=true MIR=false

Lastly, restart Protégé, and the term should be imported in ready to be used.

Refreshing imports brings in whatever changed in the source ontologies since the last refresh, so review the diff of the import modules before committing them.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
For details on what components are, please see the component section of the repository file structure document.

COHO's components are all generated from ROBOT templates, the tables in src/templates. They are listed under components in owlmake.yaml:

components:
  products:
  - filename: GWAS.owl
    use_template: true
    template_options: '--prefix "COHO: http://www.ebi.ac.uk/coho/COHO_" ...'
    templates:
    - GWAS.csv

template_options gives the prefixes the templates' CURIEs are written with (COHO:, dbpedia:, RO:, oio:).

docs.title: Editing a component
docs.text:
Never edit the files in src/ontology/components: they are rebuilt from the templates. Instead:

  1. Edit the template in src/templates (for example src/templates/GWAS.csv)
  2. Rebuild the components: 
    om make recreate-components
  3. Run the quality control checks: om make test IMP=false
  4. Commit the template and the rebuilt component together

A new component needs three more things: its entry under components in owlmake.yaml, an Import of its IRI in coho-edit.owl, and a line mapping that IRI to the file in src/ontology/catalog-v001.xml; without the last, the merge and the reasoner silently leave it out.

docs.title: Curation files
docs.text:
src/templates holds only ROBOT templates. The evidence and curatorial decisions the generated templates are built from live in src/curation: an _evidence.tsv per topic (the reviewed evidence, one row per cohort) and a _curated.tsv (hand overrides, which win). Edit the curated files, never the generated templates. All four scripts skip individuals that coho-edit.owl marks owl:deprecated, so obsoleting a term withdraws its generated assertions on the next run; its evidence rows stay as the record of what was found.

The source tables the reviews were made against are there too: ega_studies.tsv and ega_study_cohorts.tsv (EGA), gwas_catalog_cohorts.tsv.gz (GWAS Catalog), and new_cohorts_ega.tsv (the cohort names that came up in the EGA review and were not in COHO, with any consortium or parent cohort noted; new_cohorts_ega_check.tsv is their match against the list COHO was seeded from). Those names were worked through on 2026-09-22: new_cohorts_ega_decisions.tsv records, for every name on that list and every verified EGA match that no COHO term covered, whether it was minted as a new cohort (with its ID and label), resolved to an existing term, or not added and why. The minted cohorts' examples, definitions, locations and memberships were entered through the curated files, each row noting the EGA study it rests on. Refreshing a source means replacing its table and re-running the scripts. A second review, of 2026-09-23, worked through the cohort tags the GWAS Catalog and the PGS Catalog use most: pgs_catalog_cohorts.csv is the PGS Catalog's cohort list, catalog_cohort_gaps.tsv lists the PGS cohort names and GWAS Catalog cohort tags that no COHO term covered, in tiers by the number of GWAS Catalog studies that use them, and catalog_cohorts_review.tsv records the decision on each: minted as a cohort or an aggregation (with label, synonyms, type, acronym clashes, example study, definition and its drafter, location and parent, each with its source), resolved to an existing term, merged into another row as a duplicate spelling (same as), or not a cohort. Its COHO ID column records the term each row was minted as or resolved to; the examples, definitions, locations and memberships of the 108 cohorts minted from it went into the curated files, and their sub-cohort links and acronym editor notes into coho-edit.owl. After minting, each of those 108 terms was checked by independent reviewers in the same way as the second tier's (catalog_cohorts_tier_a_check.csv, with the same columns), and its applied column records what was done with each on 2026-09-23: 26 definitions were rewritten by the check and 28 given corrected sources, 57 names and 100 memberships were added, six examples or their evidence and six locations were corrected, and the Amish Complex Disease Research Program became a cohort aggregation. The review's second tier, 167 less used names, was decided and minted on the same basis on 2026-09-23: 142 new cohorts and aggregations (COHO:0000474 to COHO:0000615), among them the parent cohorts and consortia the sources named for them, with the country names their locations needed added to src/templates/gaz_xrefs.tsv. After minting, each of those 142 terms was checked by independent reviewers against the cohort's own sources: what its tags denote in the papers that use them, its definition claim by claim, its names, duplicates in COHO, its type, parent and members. catalog_cohorts_tier_b_check.csv has a row per term with its status, a verdict on its definition and each correction with its source and quote, and its applied column records what was done with each on 2026-09-23: 34 definitions were rewritten by the check, names and memberships were added, two terms were relabelled, KARE (COHO:0000529) was obsoleted as another name for the Ansan and Ansung Study (COHO:0000530), and the few corrections not applied say why. The third tier, 374 names, was drafted the same way and then, before anything was minted, checked row by row by independent reviewers, who tested what each tag denotes in the papers that use it, the cohort's own name, each claim of the definition against the cohort's sources, duplicates already in COHO, the type and the parent. Their corrections were applied to the review, and each corrected row's note ends with what the check changed ("Verified 2026-09-23: …"). The tier was minted on 2026-09-23: 330 new cohorts and aggregations (COHO:0000616 to COHO:0000945), including the two umbrella terms the check called for (the COPSAC cohorts and the ProHealth Kaiser GWAS). Its changes to terms already in COHO (the Lothian Birth Cohorts becoming the aggregation of their 1921 and 1936 cohorts, the TRAILS definition widened to both of its cohorts, memberships, acronyms, and the relabellings the check proposed and the curator accepted) are listed with their evidence in catalog_cohorts_review_existing_terms.tsv. The fourth tier, 597 names each used by one to four GWAS Catalog studies, is being worked through in a way that scales. A script matches every name against COHO's labels and synonyms and groups the names that are one cohort. A second gathers each name's evidence once, in bulk and through the EBI network: the abstracts, full texts and supplementary files of its GWAS Catalog papers (Europe PMC first, open-access text before anything else), and papers found by searching Europe PMC for the cohort's name, keeping the numbered sentences that name the cohort. A model drafts each term from those sentences alone, citing them by number, so that every quote is verbatim, and an independent reviewer checks each draft against the cohort's own sources and records its corrections as structured changes. A pilot of 50 names chosen at random was minted this way on 2026-09-24 (COHO:0000946 to COHO:0000988, 35 cohorts and 8 aggregations; three names resolved to existing terms and four are not cohorts), and the other 547 names the same day (COHO:0000989 to COHO:0001450, 462 terms, among them 15 further cohorts that a name's tag or PGS Catalog id turned out to denote; 52 names resolved to existing terms, 39 are not cohorts, 8 are spellings of another name, one waits on a name of the fifth tier). Their review rows' notes begin "Tier D (D…)", the name's key in the tier, and record what the check changed ("Checked 2026-09-24: …"). Parents that are names of the fifth tier are recorded in the note ("Parent left for later: …") and linked when that tier is minted. Many of the new aggregations have no members yet: the checks name candidate members in their notes. The fifth tier, 1,250 PGS Catalog cohort names that no GWAS Catalog study uses, goes through the same pipeline, its evidence being the papers the PGS Catalog records for each name and papers found by name, and its example a paper that used the cohort. The 220 names of the 22 batches whose checks had finished when the run paused were minted on 2026-09-24, except five whose parent or twin is a fifth-tier name not yet checked, which wait for it: 164 new terms (COHO:0001451 to COHO:0001614, 150 cohorts and 14 aggregations, among them three further cohorts that a name's PGS Catalog id turned out to denote); 28 names resolved to existing terms, 15 are not cohorts, 6 are spellings of another name and 5 are unresolved. Their review rows' notes begin "Tier E (E…)"; two rows beginning "Tier E. Late link" join fourth-tier cohorts to their new fifth-tier aggregations. The checks of the fourth and fifth tiers also found faults in terms already in COHO, which were fixed on 2026-09-24 and are recorded with their evidence in catalog_cohorts_review_existing_terms.tsv: the Cardio-metabolic Genome Epidemiology Network (COHO:0000027) became the aggregation of its member studies, COHO:0000346 was identified as the British Heart Foundation Family Heart Study and relabelled, the AA-DHS names and example moved from the Diabetes Heart Study to their own term, GENIE became a sub-cohort of H-PEACE, the Caerphilly Prospective Study took the GWAS Catalog's CaPS studies, and the definitions of the GABRIEL Advanced Surveys, the GenomeAsia 100K project and the Australian Alcohol and Nicotine Studies were corrected. The remaining fifth-tier names were not drafted: the checked ones were minted as above, those whose catalog name matches an existing term by full name, or that an earlier check tied to a minted term, were resolved to that term, obvious non-cohorts were recorded as such, and every other name became a placeholder (review notes "Placeholder: …"): an uncurated term (IAO:0000114 IAO:0000124) of the temporary unclassified class with the catalog's name, ids and other names only, in the new PGS subset (src/templates/PGS.csv). The definition, example and subset-example checks skip uncurated terms; curating a placeholder means filling it in and removing its status. src/scripts/mint_cohorts.py mints the review's decided rows from a given row on: the new terms' names, types, sub-cohort links and editor notes for shared names in coho-edit.owl, their definitions, examples, locations and memberships in the curated files, and the new COHO IDs in the review.

On 2026-09-24 a curator marked 116 terms of the cohort table in a spreadsheet with notes, comments and colours (review_2026-09-24.csv, one row per marked term with its spreadsheet row, her note, her comments and the cells she coloured). Each point was checked against the PGS Catalog, the GWAS Catalog, EGA and the papers before it was applied, and catalog_cohorts_review_existing_terms.tsv records every one with its evidence, by spreadsheet row ("review of 2026-09-24, row N"): the terms obsoleted as not cohorts (institutions, cities and local samples that the PGS Catalog names as cohorts) or as duplicates (EAS into the Edinburgh Artery Study, Nashville Biosciences into BioVU, the Manchester Cancer Research Centre into its biobank, and the Milan cohort of an EGA study whose paper gives it no name), the placeholders given their full names and, where the sources allowed, curated, the two aggregations minted (the Nurses' Health Studies, and the International Consortium on the Genetics of Heroin Dependence), the links that were already present, and the points declined (an institution is not a cohort aggregation; a placename that turns out to be a defined sample, like the Glasgow Stroke Sample, is kept and named) or left unverified.

Curating the placeholders began on 2026-09-24 with the 117 whose names the review's triage had flagged as institutions, cities or bare proper names. Each was checked against its sources without a draft, by an independent reviewer following CHECKH.md in the pipeline repository: what the PGS Catalog id denotes in the papers the Catalog records it in, whether that is a named, defined sample or only the site it came from, whether COHO already has it, and if it is a cohort its own name, definition, countries, parent and an example paper, each with a verbatim quote. The checks re-decide the placeholders' rows of catalog_cohorts_review.tsv in place (final.py --recurate), every quote is verified against the downloaded text of its URL, and src/scripts/curate_placeholders.py applies the rows: a placeholder that is a cohort or aggregation is curated under its own ID (the row's label, the catalog's name kept as a synonym, type, definition, example, locations, parent, curation status removed, PGS subset kept); one that is only an institution, city, company or unnamed local sample is obsoleted with the reason; one that is a cohort COHO already has is obsoleted with "term replaced by" that term, which takes its names and joins the PGS subset; one the sources cannot settle stays a placeholder with the check's note. Of the 117, 55 were curated as cohorts and 4 as aggregations, 41 obsoleted as not cohorts, 13 merged into existing terms (among them the Rush Memory and Aging Project, KoGES, BioMe, the Hong Kong Diabetes Register and CRCGEN) and 4 left unresolved; the names of the six countries of the Silk Road cohort were added to gaz_xrefs.tsv. A judgement the checks raised for the curator: the MalariaGEN consortium names each site's partner study ("Human genetic determinants of severe malaria in Kumasi, Ghana"), and two such names were curated as cohorts of MalariaGEN while two others of the same kind (CNRFP, MRCUTG) had been obsoleted as institutions. On 2026-09-25 the 425 placeholders the PGS Catalog links papers to were given drafted definitions without being curated: their evidence was gathered again from the enlarged cache (evidence.py), rendered in 44 batches of ten (render.py, prefix q), and drafted by one Sonnet agent per batch following DRAFT.md, from the numbered units alone; pipeline/ph_definitions.py then ran the automatic checks on every draft and lifted the definition of each draft whose verdict was a new cohort or aggregation, whose definition cited quotable units and gave no size, into definitions_curated.tsv with the cited papers as its sources, the drafter as its only contributor and a note that it is unchecked. 275 placeholders got a definition this way (one whose draft the size filter had stopped on a cholesterol threshold was added by hand); 131 had evidence too thin to define and 10 looked to the drafter like institutions rather than cohorts, 6 were drafted as duplicates of curated terms and 4 as duplicates of other placeholders, all of which is recorded per name in the pipeline repository (runs/tierD/draft/A_q*.jsonl, q_drafts.tsv) for the check that will curate them. The terms keep their uncurated status. The check followed the same day, without curating either: one Opus agent per batch, following CHECKP.md, read each cohort's papers in full and corrected its draft claim by claim, establishing the names the drafter could not define; ph_definitions.py --checked merged each check into its draft and replaced the placeholders' definition lines. A definition the checker confirmed keeps its drafter and gains the checker in the new checked by column of definitions_curated.tsv (which definitions.py writes as a second dcterms:contributor); one the checker rewrote or wrote names the checker as its drafter, with the sources it cites. Of the 425 placeholders, 381 now have a checked definition (18 confirmed, 363 rewritten or newly established) and 44 have none, because the check found them to be duplicates of curated terms (25) or of other placeholders (12), institutions rather than cohorts (7), or unresolvable from the sources (4); those verdicts, and the checks' labels, names, countries, parents, examples and the faults they noticed in existing terms, are recorded per name in the pipeline repository (check/q*.jsonl, q_checks.tsv) and wait for the curation that will promote or merge the terms. The 149 placeholders the Catalog uses in no score but whose names Europe PMC finds papers for were then checked the same way without a draft (checkrender_h.py with the prefix r, CHECKH.md, one Opus agent per batch of ten, 15 batches): 126 got a definition written by the check from the cohort's own sources, and 23 none, being institutions, registries or generic labels rather than cohorts (8), duplicates of curated terms (7) or of other placeholders (3), or names no source ties to a sample (6, among them a Toronto case-control study that six unrelated studies are called). The 220 placeholders for which neither the Catalog nor a search by name yields a paper are untouched. Three identifications that rested on the name alone (the ids Mauritius, Tianjin and Modena) were then set back to unresolved by the curator, so their placeholders have no definition. The faults the checks noticed in existing terms were verified against the sources and fixed in the same round, each recorded in catalog_cohorts_review_existing_terms.tsv: the Helmholtz term (COHO:0000165) is defined as the German lung-cancer GWAS sample it denotes and made a member of the International Lung Cancer Consortium; the CeRePP collection (COHO:0000818) is defined as the urological-cancer collection it is, bladder and kidney cases included; the SMART cohort (COHO:0000170) is relabelled with the study's own name, "Second" not "Secondary"; the Sister Study (COHO:0000660) loses the participant count from its definition and joins the Ovarian Cancer Association Consortium. The countries the checks needed (Mauritius, Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Haiti, Belarus, North Macedonia, Guernsey, Botswana and Zimbabwe) were added to gaz_xrefs.tsv. The names the checks would add to existing terms, and the merges and obsoletions, wait for the promotion, because the placeholders still carry those names.

The Global Exposome Cohort Catalogue (MOLGENIS, https://molgeniscatalogue.org/Global%20Exposome%20Cohorts) was worked through on 2026-09-25 so that every cohort it lists is in COHO and cross-referenced to its entry. Its 132 resources, read from the catalogue's API, are in src/curation/exposome_catalogue_review.tsv, a review in the same columns as the catalog review with the catalogue's id in place of the PGS id: 34 entries matched a term by name and were resolved to it (the catalogue's id, acronym and name added as synonyms); the other 98 were each checked against their sources by an independent reviewer following the pipeline repository's CHECKM.md (is it a term COHO has under another name, is it a cohort at all, and if so its own name, definition, countries, parent and an example paper, each with a verbatim quote), and every quote was verified against the downloaded text before minting. src/scripts/mint_cohorts.py --review minted the decided rows: 73 cohorts and 2 aggregations (COHO:0002596 to COHO:0002670, among them the Rotterdam Study III, the 1970 British Cohort Study, Constances, SHARE, CHARLS and the Czech arms of ELSPAC and HAPIEE), 4 more entries resolved to existing terms (the Estonian Biobank, Rotterdam Study I and II, EPIC), 7 are not cohorts (data warehouses, a registry of datasets, a funded project, a health agency, a research group and a person), and 12 are left unresolved in the review, either because no paper that used the cohort could be found or because the catalogue record was empty and the identification would rest on the id alone. The countries the new cohorts needed (Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, Luxembourg, Malta, Slovenia, Malawi and Tuvalu) were added to src/templates/gaz_xrefs.tsv. src/curation/exposome_catalogue.tsv records each entry with its COHO term, the cross-reference and the website the catalogue gives for the cohort, and src/scripts/add_xrefs.py writes those on the terms in coho-edit.owl: the entry's page in the catalogue as an oboInOwl:hasDbXref annotation, and the website, as the catalogue states it and without checking it, as an rdfs:seeAlso. The terms the catalogue lists form the GEC_subset, like the EBI resource subsets; src/scripts/catalogue_subsets.py writes its template, src/templates/GEC.csv, from the same record, and the catalogue-subset QC check holds the subset and the cross-references together.

The IHCC Cohort Atlas (https://atlas.ihccglobal.org/, the International Health Cohorts Consortium's directory of its member cohorts) was worked through the same way on 2026-09-25. Its 87 entries, read from the atlas's Arranger API (there is no page per cohort), are in src/curation/ihcc_atlas_review.tsv: 28 matched a term by label and were resolved to it, the other 59 were checked against their sources following the pipeline repository's CHECKI.md, and every quote was verified against the downloaded text before minting. mint_cohorts.py --review minted 30 cohorts and aggregations (COHO:0002671 to COHO:0002700, among them the Golestan Cohort Study, the Million Women Study, the German National Cohort, the Malaysian Cohort, Cancer Prevention Study-3, Generation Victoria, the 45 and Up Study, the South Asia Biobank, LifeGene, and the ECHO, SAPRIN, SG100K, LIFEPATH and Dementias Platform UK umbrellas with the members COHO has), and the consortium itself as a cohort aggregation, International Health Cohorts Consortium (COHO:0002701, formerly the International HundredK+ Cohorts Consortium), of which every listed cohort in COHO is a member, the atlas's listing being the source of the membership. 46 entries resolved to existing terms (among them several whose atlas entry names only the host institution, such as the Center for Applied Genomics or the Mexico City Prospective Study under its university), 5 are not cohorts (a company's research arm, a national sample store, a hospital, an institute and a cancer-control centre), and 5 stay unresolved, either for want of a paper with a PMID or because the identification would rest on the lead investigator alone. Two placeholders of the catalog review that the checks found to be an institution (NICCC) and a misspelt duplicate of the Tohoku Medical Megabank Project were obsoleted in the same round. src/curation/ihcc_atlas.tsv records each entry with its COHO term and the website the atlas gives for the cohort (the atlas has no page per cohort, so there is no cross-reference; four entries whose website field is a paper rather than a site are left without one), and add_xrefs.py writes the websites as rdfs:seeAlso on the terms, with the consortium's own site on COHO:0002701. The terms the atlas lists form the IHCC_subset (src/templates/IHCC.csv, written by catalogue_subsets.py from the record; the consortium itself is not in it), and the catalogue-subset check requires each of them to be a member of the consortium.

On 2026-09-25 the downloaded papers (the private pipeline repository's cache, and nothing else) were swept for sentences with a sub-cohort cue ("sub-cohort of", "nested within", "drawn from", "part of the" and the like) naming two COHO cohorts. The 669 candidate pairs that survived filtering were each checked against the cached text by an independent reviewer, who had to find a sentence stating that one cohort is part of the other or a member of the aggregation, and every accepted quote was verified against the cached text. src/curation/link_sweep_2026-09-25.csv is the record: one row per pair with the verdict (54 confirmed links, 10 of them sub-cohort links and 44 memberships, with their quote and source; 594 rejected, mostly cohorts merely named together or a synonym that meant something else; 5 unresolved), the reviewer's note, and the batch. Each confirmed link was then read again by the curator and, on 2026-09-25, 48 of the 54 were asserted with src/scripts/add_links.py (8 sub-cohort links into the edit file, 40 memberships into aggregation_members_curated.tsv); the applied column of the record says which, and why the other six are held (a partial overlap, links already implied through an intermediate consortium, a redundant chain, a study the text names less precisely than the sources do, and one second-hand statement). Faults in existing terms that the reviewers noticed on the way were fixed the same day and recorded in catalog_cohorts_review_existing_terms.tsv: the label of COHO:0000081 was the EGA's tag cut short (now Genetic Research in Isolated Populations, with the acronym GRIP), and National Health Service Blood and Transplant (COHO:0000123) was obsoleted as the institution through which INTERVAL recruited its donors, its GWAS Catalog example moving to INTERVAL (COHO:0000184), which the Catalog tags and which now sits in the GWAS subset.

On 2026-09-25 the number of participants of every curated cohort and aggregation was recorded, with its evidence, in src/curation/cohort_participants.csv, one row per term (1,818 rows: 1,585 cohorts and 233 aggregations). Definitions carry no sizes by design, so this table is where a cohort's size lives. The number is the one the cohort itself reports: the people enrolled or recruited, as its design or profile paper or website states it; cases and controls separately for a case-control study; the randomised participants of a trial; for an aggregation, the pooled number of its main analysis, or the number of member studies where only that is reported. It is never computed, summed or inferred, and each rests on a verbatim sentence from a source that was read (quote, with source a PMID or URL); counts says what the number counts and year the year it refers to, confidence how well the source fits, needs the closed papers that could not be read, and note the other numbers seen and why this one was chosen, or why none could be given. The batches (batch) were worked by independent reviewers from the downloaded papers and, where those gave no number, from the cohort's own pages, and every quote was then checked by script against the cached text, Europe PMC or the page: 1,407 rows give a total, 245 give cases and controls without a stated total, and 166 give no number; 1,690 quotes were found verbatim (quote verified), 102 rows carry no quote because they give no number, and 26 quotes come from supplementary spreadsheets, an infographic or page markup that the check cannot read. The numbers are asserted on the terms by the participants.owl component (see Participants below), and coho-cohorts.csv has them as columns.

docs.title: Example studies
docs.text:
Each cohort is linked to a study that used it, as an example of usage (IAO:0000112) annotation holding the study's accession (an EGA EGAS…, GWAS Catalog GCST…, MetaboLights MTBLS…, PRIDE PXD… or PGS Catalog PGS…, or the paper's PMID: where no archive study is given). A cohort in a subset needs an example from that subset's resource, which the subset-example QC check enforces, so a cohort in two subsets has two examples and one in none has one. Each example carries the study's publication as a PMID: xref on the annotation and a title as dcterms:title on it (the paper's, or the EGA study's own where it has no paper), which is what OLS shows beside the accession. Where a reviewer's evidence that the study used the cohort was verified against its source, the quote and the source URL are also on the annotation, as rdfs:comment and a second oboInOwl:hasDbXref. These come from the example_studies.owl component, whose template, src/templates/example_studies.tsv, is itself generated and should not be edited by hand:

src/scripts/example_studies.py

Paper titles are looked up in Europe PMC and kept in src/curation/example_studies_titles.tsv. The examples of the PGS subset come from the PGS Catalog: src/scripts/pgs_examples.py reads the Catalog's REST API (every score, performance metric and sample set, cached outside the repository) and gives each term a score (PGS…) that used the cohort, with the PMID and title of the publication in which it did so: a use of the cohort's own data first (a score's training samples, then a sample set a score was evaluated on), then the samples of the GWAS a score's variant associations came from, and among those the sample naming the fewest cohorts. The Catalog's record is the evidence, so the curated line carries no quote and its note says where in the record the cohort is. On 2026-09-25 the 794 placeholders were done this way: 425 were given an example (85 from training samples, 130 from evaluations, 210 from source GWAS), and 369 are cohorts the Catalog's cohort table lists but no score or evaluation uses, which the script prints and which stay without an example. The curated terms of the subset were then done with --all: 49 were given a PGS Catalog example beside the paper or GWAS Catalog example they had, and the 28 the Catalog uses in no score were taken out of the subset, recorded in subset_examples_backfill.tsv, since the subset-example check now covers the PGS subset (a placeholder is exempt and stays; --all after curating placeholders gives each newly curated term its example or takes it out). The whole of what the Catalog records is in src/curation/pgs_catalog_publications.tsv, written by src/scripts/pgs_publications.py for every live term that has a cohort id in the Catalog, not only the subset: one line per term, Catalog id and paper, the paper being a PGS Catalog publication (a score developed from the cohort's data or from its GWAS, or an evaluation of a score on it) or the source GWAS itself, with PMID, DOI, title, the Catalog's publication id and the roles the cohort has in it. The Catalog id of a term minted or resolved by the catalog review is the review's; for the cohorts COHO had before the review, the id is matched by name, exactly, to a term's label or synonym, or to the Catalog's full name for it, and the placed by column says which; an id the review found not to be a cohort is left out, and one that no term carries is printed (on 2026-09-25 two: MYBRCA and NIHR BIORESOURCE). The table then had 11,332 lines for 1,338 terms (425 placeholders, 913 curated) and 1,108 distinct PMIDs, with 188 papers the Catalog has only a DOI for. The curation pipeline's bulk fetch reads the table, so every paper the Catalog links to a term is downloaded in one run, ready for the curation of the placeholders. It reads, from src/curation, the EGA studies a human reviewed for cohort mentions (ega_studies.tsv, with their verified matches in ega_study_cohorts.tsv) and the GWAS Catalog's studies with one cohort per line (gwas_catalog_cohorts.tsv.gz, a Catalog export of 2026-09). How a study is chosen is described at the top of the script.

Cohorts the script finds no study for are printed, some with a candidate study that matched on an acronym alone and needs a curator to confirm it, and so are subset members that lack an example from their subset's resource, with the studies the tables suggest. To give a cohort an example by hand, or to overrule the script's choice, add a line to src/curation/example_studies_curated.tsv (tab-separated columns ID, example study, PMID, note, and optionally quote and URL, the verbatim evidence that the study used the cohort and where it was read) and run the script again. There is one line per example: a cohort with curated lines gets exactly those examples and no automatic one, so a cohort that needs a second example has both written there. A line with a PMID and no accession gives the paper itself as the example. A line with both left empty rejects the script's choice without replacing it: acronyms are shared between cohorts (the GWAS Catalog's ACP on GCST90281184 is an Amish cohort, not the Asian Cancer Project), so a match on one is not always right. The current curated rows come from two reviews of every cohort on 2026-09-22, merged into src/curation/example_studies_evidence.tsv (one row per cohort: verdict, accession, PMID, evidence quote, source URL, whether the quote was verified, confidence, and the reviewer's remark); accessions, PMIDs and quotes were checked against Europe PMC, PMC, the GWAS Catalog and EGA before being accepted.

docs.title: Data collection locations
docs.text: Where a cohort's participants were recruited is asserted with has_data_collection_location, to a country or region from the gaz_xrefs.owl component, by the locations.owl component. Its template, src/templates/locations.tsv, is generated by src/scripts/locations.py from src/curation/location_evidence.tsv (a review of every assertion, one row per cohort with the countries asserted, a verdict — correct, incomplete, wrong, unverified, or unlocated for a cohort COHO had not placed — the right countries, the evidence and whether its quote was verified; an unlocated row with no countries records why none could be given) and src/curation/location_curated.tsv (overrides: ID, countries as pipe-separated dbpedia resource names, quote, URL, note; an empty countries removes the cohort's locations, and a cohort may have several rows, one per quote, each attaching its quote to its own countries). Where the evidence quote was verified in its source, it goes on the assertion as rdfs:comment, with the source URL as oboInOwl:hasDbXref. The location is where participants were recruited, not where the data were analysed or are held. A country the review needs that gaz_xrefs.tsv lacks must be added there first, with its GAZ xref and continent; the script refuses to run otherwise. The script lists the individuals in coho-edit.owl that have no location, so the gaps are visible after each run.

docs.title: Participants
docs.text: The number of participants a cohort reports is asserted on it by the participants.owl component as numberOfParticipants, with numberOfCases and numberOfControls where its source gives cases and controls separately (and only those where no source states a total). Each is an integer annotation carrying its evidence as annotations on the assertion: the verbatim sentence stating the number (rdfs:comment), the source it came from (oboInOwl:hasDbXref, a PMID or a URL) and what the number counts and the year it refers to (IAO:0000116). The template, src/templates/participants.tsv, is generated by src/scripts/participants.py from src/curation/cohort_participants.csv, the record described above; a row with no number gives nothing, and a quote the check could not find in its source is left off, so the number stands with its source and note alone. Definitions never give a size: the number lives here, as the source states it and never computed, and the participants-evidence check requires every number to carry its source. coho-cohorts.csv has the three numbers and their sources as columns.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Each cohort's textual definition (IAO:0000115) comes from the definitions.owl component, generated by src/scripts/definitions.py from src/curation/definitions_evidence.tsv (one row per cohort: the definition, its source, a supporting quote and whether the quote was found in the source) and src/curation/definitions_curated.tsv (overrides; an empty definition withholds one). The cohorts to define are the individuals declared in coho-edit.owl, so a newly minted cohort is reported as undefined until a row is added for it. Each definition carries its source as IAO:0000119 (the paper's PMID, or the URL of the cohort's own site; a definition drawn from several sources lists them separated by | in the curated file and carries one IAO:0000119 for each) and, as dcterms:contributor, the agents that drafted and checked it: the definitions were written by an AI model from sources it retrieved and checked by another against those sources, and the annotations say so on every one. A definition supplied through the curated file carries only its drafter's annotation, taken from the file's optional drafted by column (for example "Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), 2026-09" for the cohorts minted from the GWAS and PGS Catalog review); where that column is empty, the definition was written by the checking model alone and names it. The curated definitions have no checked by contributor. Those of the catalog review's third, fourth and fifth tiers were checked against the cohorts' sources by independent reviewers before minting, and those of its second tier after minting (the check rewrote the ones it found wanting), as the curated file's note on each says; the rest have not been checked by a second model or person. src/curation/type_changes.tsv lists the cohorts whose type (cohort or cohort aggregation) the drafting suggested changing, and which were applied.

docs.title: Aggregation members
docs.text: A cohort aggregation is linked to each cohort it combines, and to each aggregation it includes, by hasCohort, from the aggregation_members.owl component generated by src/scripts/aggregation_members.py from src/curation/aggregation_members_evidence.tsv (one row per aggregation and member from a review of every aggregation's membership: the member as its source names it, its COHO ID where it exists or "new", the source, a quote, whether the quote was verified, and per aggregation whether the listed members are cohorts at all — sources that list countries, sites or institutions are marked include = no) and src/curation/aggregation_members_curated.tsv (overrides; a note beginning "remove" drops a membership). Only members that exist in COHO are asserted; the others are the input to minting new cohorts, after which re-running the script links them. Each assertion carries the quote naming the member as rdfs:comment and the source URL as oboInOwl:hasDbXref.

docs.title: Adding a component
docs.text:
1. Create the template, src/templates/your-component-name.tsv (or .csv)
  2. Add the component to the components list in owlmake.yaml, as above
  3. Bring the repository into step with owlmake.yaml: 
    om update-repo
    This adds the component to the imports of the edit file (src/ontology/coho-edit.owl), tells the XML catalog (src/ontology/catalog-v001.xml) where its IRI is to be found, so that Protégé and the build can load it, and creates a placeholder src/ontology/components/your-component-name.owl.
  4. Build it: om make recreate-components

Removing a component is the same in reverse: take it out of owlmake.yaml, run om update-repo, and delete its file.

A component can also be derived from SSSOM mappings (use_mappings: true with a list of mappings) or fetched from a remote resource (source: https://example.org/component-source.owl). One that is generated by a process of its own is described as a target, see Build configuration.
